# Joshua 12 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter functions as a summary catalogue of all the kings defeated by Israel, both east of the Jordan under Moses (vv. 1–6) and west of the Jordan under Joshua (vv. 7–24). It serves as a bridge between the conquest narratives (chs. 1–11) and the land distribution that follows (chs. 13–21). The chapter is essentially a written memorial — a "royal roster of doom" — that testifies to God's faithfulness in keeping His covenant promise to give the land to Abraham's descendants.

**Matthew Henry** describes it as "a summary of Israel's conquests," coming in "not only as a conclusion of the history of the wars of Canaan...but as a preface to the history of the dividing of Canaan." *(https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/12.htm)*

**John Calvin** says: "There is very good reason for here placing before our eyes as it were a living picture of the goodness of God, proving that there had been a complete ratification and performance of the covenant made with Abraham." *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-12.html)*

**Keil & Delitzsch** note that in the earlier battle narratives, only the kings who formed leagues against Israel were named; this chapter now provides "a detailed list…of all the kings that were slain" to give "a complete picture of all the victories which Israel had gained under the omnipotent help of its God." *(https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-12-commentary)*

---

## Verses 1–6: Kings Conquered East of the Jordan under Moses

### v. 1 — Introduction to the Transjordan conquests
> *"Now these are the kings of the land whom the Israelites struck down and whose lands they took beyond the Jordan to the east, from the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon, including all the Arabah eastward:"*

- **Gill** notes the phrase "on the other side Jordan toward the rising of the sun" refers to the east side of the land of Canaan. The Arnon was the border between Moab and the Amorites (Num. 21:13); from there to Mount Hermon lay the territory of the two Amorite kings. *(https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/12.htm)*

- **Guzik** (charismatic/Pentecostal) comments that this list "only seems tedious to modern readers because they are distant from these great victories. For those who received their inheritance in the land of these kings, these were essential matters that touched everyday life, answering the question: 'What land belongs to Israel?'" *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

- **Precept Austin** adds a spiritual application: "If He did it for Israel to whom He promised the land, He will do it for believers to whom He has promised an abundant life in Christ (Jn 10:10b)." The chapter is "a monument to the great faithfulness of the LORD to keep His covenant promises." *(https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-12-commentary)*

- **Cyril Barber** (cited at Precept Austin) observes that by including the Transjordan victories, the writer safeguards "against the fear that those tribes that had been given an inheritance in Transjordan would (1) forget their ties to the rest of God's people…or (2) be looked upon by their brethren in Canaan with disfavor." *(https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-12-commentary)*

### vv. 2–3 — Sihon king of the Amorites
> *"Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon. He ruled from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley…up to the Jabbok River…that is, half of Gilead, as well as the Arabah east of the Sea of Chinnereth to the Sea of the Arabah…"*

- **Guzik** highlights that Numbers 21:21–32 records this defeat. Notably, "God hardened the spirit and made obstinate the heart of Sihon, ensuring his defeat (Deuteronomy 2:30)." Yet Guzik adds a theological nuance: "It was not unrighteous of God to harden Sihon because he was not originally favorable towards Israel. God did not change Sihon's heart to make him attack Israel. God simply gave Sihon over to what his evil heart desired." *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

- **Gill** notes that Heshbon was Sihon's capital, which he had taken from the Moabites (Num. 21:26). He points out that "half Gilead belonged to the kingdom of Sihon, as the other half did to the kingdom of Og, as in Joshua 12:5." *(https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/12.htm)*

- **Ellicott** directs readers to Deuteronomy 2:31–37 for the fuller description of Sihon's territory. *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-12.html)*

- **Thompson** (cited at Precept Austin) portrays Sihon as "a power-crazed ruler…Sihon represents the big and powerful enemy who blatantly tries to prevent God's people from getting to where God wants them to be. Sihon-types will be defeated, no matter how impressive they may appear to be." *(https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-12-commentary)*

### vv. 4–5 — Og king of Bashan
> *"And Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived in Ashtaroth and Edrei. He ruled over Mount Hermon, Salecah, all of Bashan up to the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and half of Gilead to the border of Sihon king of Heshbon."*

- **Guzik** emphasizes that Og was "of the remnant of the giants" — Deuteronomy 3:11 notes his iron bed measured about 13½ feet long, indicating his extraordinary size. The battle with Og is recorded in Numbers 21:33–35. Israel did not provoke this battle, but "through their God they won a glorious victory." *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

- **Gill** notes Og dwelt at both Ashtaroth and Edrei, both royal cities. "Ashtaroth" was named after the goddess Astarte, worshipped there. *(https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/12.htm)*

- **Matthew Henry** observes that Og "had palaces in both, and resided sometimes in one and sometimes in the other; one perhaps was his summer seat and the other his winter seat. But Israel took both from him, and made one grave to serve him that could not be content with one palace." *(https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/12.htm)*

- **Ellicott** makes a striking observation about vv. 6–7 together: "There are two kings reckoned to Moses, and thirty-one to Joshua; making a total of thirty-three. Yet the two slain by Moses are individually represented as far greater than any who are named in this book. And in the Psalms…we have 'Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og the king of Bashan' expressed by name, and the rest only summarised as 'all the kingdoms of Canaan' (Psalms 135:11-12; 136:19-20)." *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-12.html)*

### v. 6 — The eastern lands deeded to Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh
> *"Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the Israelites had struck them down and given their land as an inheritance to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh."*

- **Guzik** notes: "These conquests were achieved while Israel was still on the eastern side of the Jordan River. Israel's wars of conquest and judgment did not begin with Joshua." Half of Manasseh lived east of the Jordan, half west — a distribution described in Numbers 32. *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

- **Ellicott** points out a typological reading: "The analogy between the work of Moses and Joshua in this literal conquest, and the work of Moses and the true Joshua in respect of the inheritance of the Church of God, which was partly won before the passage of Jordan—i.e., before the death of Christ—but much more afterwards, is too plain to be overlooked." *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-12.html)*

- **Matthew Henry** draws a similar law/gospel parallel: "Moses, in his time, gave to one part of Israel a very rich and fruitful country, but it was on the outside of Jordan; but Joshua gave to all Israel the holy land, the mountain of God's sanctuary, within Jordan: so the law conferred upon some few of God's spiritual Israel external temporal blessings, which were earnests of good things to come; but our Lord Jesus, the true Joshua, has provided for all the children of promise spiritual blessings." *(https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/12.htm)*

---

## Verses 7–8: Introduction to Kings Conquered West of the Jordan under Joshua

### v. 7 — Scope of the western conquest
> *"And these are the kings of the land that Joshua and the Israelites conquered beyond the Jordan to the west, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir…"*

- **Guzik** cites Madvig: "East of the Jordan there were only two kings, each of whom ruled a wide area with many cities. The land west of the Jordan was divided into individual city-states. Israel's conquests on both sides of the Jordan are mentioned together here to emphasize the unity of the nation." *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

- **Ellicott** also notes: "the continuity of the work of Moses and Joshua should be noticed. The land which God gave to Israel is made up of two portions…But the conquest of Canaan is one enterprise, begun by Moses and finished by Joshua." *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-12.html)*

- **Matthew Henry** comments: "The boundaries are more largely described, Num. 34:2, etc. But what is here said is enough to show that God had been as good as his word, and had given them possession of all he had promised them by Moses, if they would but have kept it." *(https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/12.htm)*

### v. 8 — The types of land and peoples conquered
> *"the hill country, the foothills, the Arabah, the slopes, the wilderness, and the Negev—the lands of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites"*

- **Matthew Henry** notes the diverse geography: mountains that were "not craggy, and rocky, and barren, but fruitful hills…valleys, not mossy and boggy, but covered with corn…even in that rich land there were wildernesses too, or forests…which served as foils to set off the more pleasant and fruitful countries." He also points out that six nations are listed here, not the seven of Deuteronomy 7:1 — the Girgashites are omitted. He cites a Jewish tradition that says "upon the approach of Israel under Joshua they all withdrew and went into Africa." *(https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/12.htm)*

- **Precept Austin** adds from Woudstra: "By enumerating the kings conquered by Joshua and Israel, the writer gives eloquent testimony to the fact that Israel's enemies, who had banded together with hostile intent (Josh 11:19-20; cf. Josh 9:1-2; 11:1-5), had been unable to stand against Israel and its God. Thus seen, this list is a song of praise to the Lord's honor." *(https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-12-commentary)*

- **J. Vernon McGee** (dispensational, cited at StudyLight): "a chapter like this, the thing that it impresses upon me, is the detail that the God of this universe has given to items like this…God gets right down to the nitty-gritty, right where you and I live. We sometimes hesitate to take to God in prayer so many of the details of our lives…talk to Him about it." *(https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/12-12.html)*

---

## Verses 9–24: The List of Thirty-One Conquered Kings

### General observations on the list

- **Ellicott** explains the list follows the order of conquest: first Jericho and Ai (v. 9); then the southern campaign kings from Jerusalem (v. 10) through Makkedah (v. 16); then the central/northern campaign from Bethel (v. 16b) through Tirzah (v. 24). He notes several kings "have not been previously mentioned in Joshua, nor is the capture of Jarmuth mentioned" — this list therefore supplements the earlier narratives. *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-12.html)*

- **Guzik** emphasizes the historical reliability: "These descriptions are also important because they make it clear that these things happened at a real time, and in real places. These are not fairy tales that begin with 'once upon a time.'" He cites Hess: "Conquest lists of Ancient Near Eastern kings have been compared. Close comparisons exist between this list and those composed for Pharaohs who campaigned in Palestine." *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

- **Dr. Constable** (dispensational): "Many of the same names appear in the Amarna letters, thus confirming the historicity of our text." Also notes that sites like Shechem and Dothan are missing: "Here is evidence that the conquests of the hill country are not recorded in the narratives of Joshua." *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-12.html)*

- **Matthew Henry** makes three observations: (1) The large number of kings (31) shows "what a very fruitful country Canaan then was, which could support so many kingdoms." (2) Each king ruled a small city-state — "what narrow limits men's ambition was then confined to." (3) It demonstrates "how good God was to Israel, in giving them victory over all these kings." Henry then provides a detailed breakdown of which kingdoms fell to which tribes. *(https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joshua/12.htm)*

- **Guzik** quotes Clarke: "In ancient times all kings had very small territories. Every village or town had its chief; and this chief was independent of his neighbours, and exercised regal power in his own district." *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

### v. 9 — Jericho and Ai
> *"the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is near Bethel, one"*

- These are the first two conquests recorded in Joshua 6–8. Their placement at the head of the list confirms the chronological ordering.

### v. 10 — Jerusalem and Hebron
> *"the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one"*

- Jerusalem's king was Adoni-zedek, leader of the southern coalition (Josh. 10). Hebron's king was Hoham (Josh. 10:3). **Ellicott** notes Jerusalem was not fully occupied until David's time, yet its king was defeated in battle. *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-12.html)*

### vv. 11–12 — Jarmuth, Lachish, Eglon, Gezer
- Part of the southern coalition (Josh. 10). **Ellicott** notes that the capture of Jarmuth was not previously narrated in Joshua. The king of Gezer (Horam) came to help Lachish and was defeated (Josh. 10:33).

### vv. 13–15 — Debir, Geder, Hormah, Arad, Libnah, Adullam
- **Ellicott** identifies Geder with Jedûr in the Hebron mountains (Josh. 15:58). Hormah and Arad are interesting: both appear in Numbers 21:1–3 where Arad, after destruction, is called Hormah. Ellicott suggests "it is possible that the Hormah and Arad of this chapter may both be of the number. Or they may be different places." *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-12.html)*

### vv. 16–18 — Makkedah, Bethel, Tappuah, Hepher, Aphek, Lasharon
- **Precept Austin** notes Bethel marks "the geographical transition in this list from the territory conquered in the southern campaign of Joshua, to that which he conquered in his northern campaign." *(https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-12-commentary)*

- **Ellicott** says Tappuah is probably the one in Ephraim (Josh. 16:8). Hepher is unidentified but possibly Gath-hepher in Zebulun. "Aphek is a name belonging to six different towns." For Lasharon, Ellicott suggests reading it as "to the Sharon" (the definite article form), meaning "the king of that district" of the Sharon plain. *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-12.html)*

### vv. 19–20 — Madon, Hazor, Shimron-meron, Achshaph
- Hazor was the head of the northern coalition (Josh. 11). Jabin its king was defeated and Hazor burned. **Ellicott** identifies Achshaph as probably El-Yasif in Asher. *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-12.html)*

### vv. 21–23 — Taanach, Megiddo, Kedesh, Jokneam, Dor, Goiim in Gilgal
- **Ellicott**: Taanach (Tânah) in Issachar but assigned to Manasseh (Josh. 17:11). Megiddo became famous later in Israel's history. Kedesh is probably Kedesh-Naphtali (Kedes). Jokneam in Carmel is Tell Keimûn. Dor is Tantûra (on the coast). Gilgal here is probably Jiljilieh in the Sharon plain. *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-12.html)*

### v. 24 — Tirzah and the total
> *"and the king of Tirzah, one. So there were thirty-one kings in all."*

- **Guzik** notes Tirzah "was the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel until the time of Omri (1 Kings 14:17; 15:21, 33; 16:6–24)." *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

- **Ellicott** places Tirzah as Teiasîr in Manasseh. *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-12.html)*

- **Guzik** summarizes the purpose of the total: "This list gave a way for Israel to forever remember the great things God had done for them. In written form, this list served a similar function as the memorial from the crossing of the Jordan (Joshua 4:1-9)." He quotes Redpath: "Sometimes in the course of human experience it is good to sit down and reflect on what has been conquered by the grace of God. Not boastfully, but with a humble and grateful heart." *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

- **Guzik** also offers a sober balance: "With all these kings conquered, with every one of these principalities and powers over the land defeated, there was no doubt that the land belonged to Israel. Nevertheless, the individual tribes still had much to possess for their own." Quoting Morgan: "The chosen people are now seen in actual possession of the land. The destructive part of the divine work was accomplished. The constructive purposes of God might now go forward." *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### The question of "defeated" vs. "fully conquered"

A point of debate centers on whether the chapter claims total conquest when later passages indicate many cities were not fully occupied until much later (cf. Josh. 15:63; 17:12; Jdg. 1:22, 29).

- **Norman Geisler** (evangelical apologist, cited at Precept Austin) addresses this directly: "There is a difference between defeating a king's army on the field of battle and later destroying his capital city. Once defeated in battle, the king and his remaining troops would retreat to their stronghold where it was much more difficult to root them out. Sudden victory and permanent vanquishing are two different things. So understood, there is absolutely no contradiction between these texts." *(https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-12-commentary)*

- **The Bridgeway Bible Commentary** (dispensational) takes a similar approach: "Once Israel had won control of the land as a whole, Israel's leaders began the task of dividing it among the tribes. Throughout the country, however, there were many areas that the Canaanites still occupied…The individual Israelite tribes were now to clear the Canaanites out of these areas and so enjoy full possession of their inheritance." *(https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/12-12.html)*

- **Chuck Smith** (Calvary Chapel, dispensational): "Now we had in chapter 12…the roster of the kings of Canaan…frankly, this to me is not exciting…but a chapter like this, the thing that it impresses upon me, is the detail that the God of this universe has given to items like this." *(https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/12-12.html)*

### Reformed / Calvinist emphasis

- **John Calvin** emphasizes that this chapter is a "living image of the grace of God" demonstrating covenant fulfillment. He focuses on the supernatural character of the victories: "In this aged man [Joshua] how could there be so much vigor as to fit him for carrying on so many wars…had not celestial virtue furnished him with more than mortal strength?" The list proves God's direct intervention. *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-12.html)*

- **Gill** (Reformed Baptist) provides meticulous geographic and textual detail, noting connections to Numbers and Deuteronomy. His focus is on the precise boundaries and the fulfillment of the land promise. *(https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joshua/12.htm)*

### Pentecostal/Charismatic emphasis

- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) applies the chapter to the believer's spiritual warfare: "We should take time to reflect on what God has conquered and accomplished in our lives, not boastfully but with humble and grateful hearts." The conquests are a pattern for "possessing your possessions" in Christ. *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

- **Precept Austin** echoes this with a quote from Today in the Word (Moody): "The battle for our spiritual inheritance has already been fought and won by Jesus Christ. The question we must ask ourselves is, have we claimed it? Have we 'apportioned' the spoils of Christ's victory?" *(https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-12-commentary)*

### Anglican / Ellicott's typological reading

- **Ellicott** draws a typological parallel between Moses/Joshua and Law/Gospel, with the Jordan representing death to self or the death of Christ. The two portions of Israel's inheritance — one before crossing Jordan, one after — prefigure the partial inheritance under the old covenant and the fuller inheritance under Christ. *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-12.html)*

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

- **Butler** (cited by Constable at StudyLight): "The description was not complete. Shechem is not mentioned, and the hills of Ephraim are sparsely represented, as is the territory north of Hazor. Completeness is not the object. The writer seeks to compile a list that will impress the readers with the greatness of the feat of God in working for Israel." *(https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/joshua-12.html)*

- **Hess** (cited by Guzik): "Conquest lists of Ancient Near Eastern kings have been compared. Close comparisons exist between this list and those composed for Pharaohs who campaigned in Palestine." This supports the genre of the chapter as an authentic ancient Near Eastern royal inscription pattern. *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

- **Howard** (cited by Guzik): The importance of the lists "lies in confirming the veracity of the claims elsewhere that these lands were indeed conquered, in confirming the tribes' claims to the lands mentioned here, and in confirming that God was faithful to his promises to give these lands to his people." *(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-12/)*

- **Woudstra** (cited at Precept Austin): "Structurally it is closely related to Josh 11:16-17…this list is a song of praise to the Lord's honor." *(https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-12-commentary)*
